models.model_label: Forecast revision response by analyst ability group (80% threshold)
models.sample_description: Individual analyst forecast revision events for one-year-ahead annual earnings announced in 1990–1994. The data intersect Compustat, CRSP and I/B/E/S; events require the relevant earnings, three-day return-window, prior analyst-firm forecast-ability and forecast-surprise data. Firms must have at least five brokerage houses following them in each year 1988–1994, and each analyst-firm pair must have at least five forecasts in the preceding two years with at least one in each year. The three-day revision window must not overlap another same-firm revision, earnings announcement or dividend declaration. The final sample has 15,446 revision events.
models.method_details: The source presents a regression equation and coefficient t-statistics, but does not identify OLS or another underlying estimator; no estimator is inferred from the linear form.

dependent_variable.name: R_ijt
dependent_variable.definition: Three-day market-adjusted return for firm i surrounding the announcement of analyst j’s earnings forecast on day t, over days −1, 0 and +1. The source does not give the arithmetic formula for the market adjustment.

evidence.quote: Three-day market-adjusted return [−1 , 0 , +1] surrounding the announcement of an earnings forecast for firm i by analyst j on day t

independent_variables.name: FR_ijt × SUP_ijt
independent_variables.definition: Forecast surprise multiplied by SUP_ijt, which is one if analyst j is classified as superior for firm i at time t and zero otherwise. Forecast surprise is the analyst’s current EPS forecast less the same analyst’s most recent EPS forecast for the same firm, divided by firm i’s share price two days before the revision. At the selected 80% threshold, superior means 80% or more of that analyst’s forecasts for the firm in the preceding two years were closer to actual earnings than the contemporaneous I/B/E/S consensus. Table 4 also places equality at 80% in the normal range, so assignment at that boundary is unresolved.
independent_variables.formula: (EPS forecast for firm i by analyst j on day t − most recent EPS forecast for firm i by analyst j) / firm i share price two days before the revision × SUP_ijt

An analyst is defined as being superior with respect to a certain firm at a given point in time if 80% or more of the analyst’s forecasts for that firm in the preceding two years were closer to actual earnings than was the contemporaneous I/B/E/S consensus forecast.

scope.quote: We empirically identify superior analysts using their past forecasting track record for a specific firm’s earnings and demonstrate that subsequent forecast announcements by these superior analysts have a greater impact on security prices than do the forecasts of other analysts.

The empirical tests for an impact of analyst forecasting ability on the price reaction to forecast revision announcements are presented in section 3. Section 4 reports the results of tests to identify a forecasting ability spillover effect and the time period in which prior forecasting ability is relatively more important.
An explicit comparison of the announcement return effect of forecasts by superior, normal, and inferior analysts is reported in table 4.
In order to establish whether the results are sensitive to the 80% threshold chosen, we also report test results using 90% and 70% thresholds.
To maintain a larger sample of superior analysts, the 80% threshold measure will be used in the subsequent tests in this paper.

review_notes: Scope decision from the source: Table 4 Model at the selected 80% ability threshold is the principal direct comparison of forecast-revision price responses for superior, normal, and inferior analysts. The paper calls 90% and 70% cutoffs sensitivity checks and says the 80% measure is used in subsequent tests. Table 2 is the overall surprise relationship; Table 3 restricts the sample to superior analysts; Tables 5–6 are later spillover/timing tests, so they are excluded.

The supplied reading has a broken equation transcription on physical page 9. The exact table equation was visually inspected in a crop of PDF page 9 (vector/text equation; the frozen render_equations helper found no embedded-image candidate): intercept plus FR×SUP, FR×NOR, and FR×INF only. No component-only main effects were added; the reading was not edited.
The Table 4 category labels overlap at the 20% and 80% boundaries (normal 20–80%, inferior 20% and below, superior 80% and above); the paper does not resolve assignment at those equalities.
results_review_notes: Only the frozen Table 4 full-sample 80% threshold result set is retained. The 90% and 70% sensitivity columns, Table 3 superior-only regressions, and later spillover/timing models are excluded.
The selected model contains three forecast-surprise-by-analyst-category interaction terms and an intercept; no standalone forecast-surprise term or other controls appear in the displayed equation.

The three-day market-adjusted return is reported as the outcome; its market-adjustment formula is not supplied. The frozen base also records overlapping category boundaries at 20% and 80%, which remain unresolved.

Table 4 reports t-statistics in parentheses for coefficients and F-statistics/p-values for pairwise coefficient differences. Coefficient t-statistics are retained with unknown sidedness and degrees of freedom. The pairwise F tests are represented as auxiliary contrasts, not as individual coefficient inference.

Table 1 provides the number and percentage of revisions by superior analysts at the 80% threshold, which is an upstream SUP component of the retained interaction. No descriptive mean for raw forecast surprise, market-adjusted return, normal-analyst status or inferior-analyst status was found in the assigned reading.
